entries.title: TDS on salary
entries.body: Every employer paying taxable salary to an employee must deduct TDS at the time of payment. There is no fixed rate; tax is deducted at the employee's average rate of income-tax computed on estimated salary for the year under the applicable slab (old or new regime).
entries.rate: Average rate of income-tax on estimated total salary (i.e. the employee's slab rate, including surcharge and cess as applicable). No single flat rate.
entries.rate_no_pan: Sec 206AA applies — TDS at the higher of the rate in force or 20% (in practice 20% if estimated tax works out lower), but cannot exceed the slab computation in most salary cases. CA should confirm treatment for the specific employee.
entries.threshold: No fixed monetary threshold. TDS arises only if estimated annual salary exceeds the basic exemption limit after considering eligible deductions/rebate (e.g. sec 87A rebate up to Rs 12 lakh taxable income under the new regime for FY 2025-26 onwards means many employees have nil tax).
entries.payer: Employer (any person responsible for paying salary)

sources.name: ClearTax — TDS & TCS changes from April 2026

entries.caveats: Rate depends entirely on the employee's regime choice and slab; the new tax regime (with sec 87A rebate making income up to Rs 12 lakh effectively tax-free for FY 2025-26 onwards) is now the default. IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CHANGE: the Income-tax Act 1961 was repealed w.e.f. 01-04-2026 and replaced by the Income-tax Act 2025; salary TDS is now governed by Sec 392 (TDS challans/returns use new payment codes, not the label '192'). The label '192' is retained here only because it remains the universally-used reference. CA must confirm regime, exemption limit and rebate for the specific employee and use the correct new-Act section/code when filing.

entries.title: TDS on premature EPF withdrawal
entries.body: When the trustees of the EPF scheme (or the EPFO) pay an employee the accumulated PF balance before five years of continuous service, TDS is deducted. Applies only to taxable premature withdrawals.
entries.rate: 10% on the taxable accumulated balance
entries.rate_no_pan: 20% (Sec 206AA). NOTE: the earlier 'maximum marginal rate if no PAN' rule was removed by the Finance Act 2023 (w.e.f. 01-04-2023); it is now 20%, not MMR.
entries.threshold: Rs 50,000 (aggregate taxable withdrawal in the year). No TDS if the taxable amount is below Rs 50,000.
entries.payer: Trustees of the EPF scheme / EPFO (person paying the accumulated balance)

entries.title: TDS on interest on securities
entries.body: Any person paying a resident interest on securities (e.g. debentures, government securities) must deduct TDS at the time of credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.threshold: Rs 10,000 per financial year (raised from Rs 5,000 by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025). For specific securities such as 8% Savings (Taxable) Bonds / Floating Rate Savings Bonds the threshold is Rs 10,000; debentures of a listed company paid to an individual/HUF also have a Rs 10,000 limit.
entries.payer: Person paying interest on securities (company, government, etc.)
entries.caveats: General threshold raised to Rs 10,000 w.e.f. 01-04-2025 (Finance Act 2025). Several security-type-specific thresholds and exemptions exist (e.g. certain government securities, dematerialised listed securities) — CA should confirm the exact limit for the specific security. Now governed by Sec 393(1) of the Income-tax Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2026.

entries.title: TDS on dividend
entries.body: An Indian company (or a company in which the public is substantially interested) paying dividend to a resident shareholder must deduct TDS before making the payment.
entries.threshold: Rs 10,000 per financial year per shareholder (raised from Rs 5,000 by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025).
entries.payer: Indian company / principal officer paying the dividend
entries.caveats: Threshold raised from Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000 w.e.f. 01-04-2025 (Finance Act 2025). Applies to dividends paid to residents; dividends to non-residents fall under Sec 195. Now governed by Sec 393(1) of the Income-tax Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2026.

entries.title: TDS on interest other than securities
entries.body: Any person (other than individual/HUF not under tax audit) paying a resident interest other than interest on securities — e.g. bank fixed-deposit interest, interest on loans — must deduct TDS at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.threshold: Where payer is a bank, co-operative society engaged in banking, or post office: Rs 50,000 per year (Rs 1,00,000 for senior citizens). In all other cases: Rs 10,000 per year. (Bank/senior thresholds raised by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025; previously Rs 40,000 / Rs 50,000.)
entries.payer: Payer of interest (banks, co-operative societies, post offices, companies, firms; individuals/HUF only if under tax audit in the preceding year)

entries.title: TDS on payments to contractors
entries.body: Any specified person paying a resident contractor/sub-contractor for carrying out any work (including supply of labour) under a contract must deduct TDS at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.rate: 1% if payee is an individual or HUF; 2% if payee is any other person (company, firm, etc.)
entries.threshold: Rs 30,000 per single contract/payment, OR Rs 1,00,000 in aggregate during the financial year. If aggregate crosses Rs 1,00,000, TDS applies on all payments including earlier sub-Rs 30,000 ones. (Aggregate limit was raised from Rs 75,000 to Rs 1,00,000 by the Finance Act 2024 w.e.f. 01-04-2025; single-payment limit unchanged at Rs 30,000.)
entries.payer: Specified persons (companies, firms, government, individuals/HUF under tax audit, etc.)
entries.caveats: Rates (1%/2%) unchanged in Budget 2025. Aggregate annual threshold is Rs 1,00,000 (raised from Rs 75,000 w.e.f. 01-04-2025); single-transaction threshold Rs 30,000. Special exemption: no TDS to a transporter (goods carriage) owning <=10 vehicles who furnishes PAN and a declaration. Now governed by Sec 393(1) of the Income-tax Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2026. CA should confirm the new-Act payment code and whether 'manpower/labour supply' is treated under the new contractor sub-table (some FY 2026-27 commentary references a 1%/2% manpower-services entry that should be verified).

entries.title: TDS on insurance commission
entries.body: Any person paying a resident remuneration or reward by way of commission for soliciting or procuring insurance business must deduct TDS at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.rate: 2% if payee is a resident other than a company; 10% if payee is a domestic company. (Rate for non-company residents reduced from 5% to 2% by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025.)
entries.threshold: Rs 20,000 per financial year (raised from Rs 15,000 by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025).
entries.payer: Insurer / person paying insurance commission

entries.title: TDS on life-insurance payout
entries.body: Any person paying a resident a sum under a life-insurance policy (maturity/surrender proceeds) that is NOT exempt under sec 10(10D) must deduct TDS. Tax is on the income component only, not the gross payout.
entries.rate: 2% on the income component (payout minus total premiums paid). Reduced from 5% to 2% by the Finance Act 2024 w.e.f. 01-10-2024.
entries.threshold: Rs 1,00,000 (aggregate non-exempt payout under the policy in the financial year). No TDS if the aggregate is below Rs 1,00,000.
entries.payer: Insurer making the policy payout

entries.title: TDS on rent
entries.body: Any person (other than individual/HUF not under tax audit) paying a resident rent for the use of plant/machinery/equipment, or land/building/furniture/fittings, must deduct TDS at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.rate: 2% for use of plant, machinery or equipment [sec 194-I(a)]; 10% for use of land, building (incl. factory building), furniture or fittings [sec 194-I(b)].
entries.threshold: Rs 6,00,000 per financial year (raised from Rs 2,40,000 by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025). Several sources describe it as a Rs 50,000-per-month basis, but the statutory limit is expressed as Rs 6,00,000 per year per payee.
entries.payer: Person paying rent (companies, firms, individuals/HUF under tax audit)
entries.caveats: Threshold raised from Rs 2,40,000 to Rs 6,00,000 per year w.e.f. 01-04-2025 (Finance Act 2025) — many charts (incl. some FY 2026-27 ones) still show Rs 2,40,000 (stale); this is a common error point. CA should VERIFY whether the limit is applied per-annum (Rs 6,00,000) or per-month (Rs 50,000) for borderline cases — sources phrase it both ways. Rates (2% / 10%) unchanged. Distinct from 194-IB (rent paid by small individuals/HUF). Now governed by Sec 393(1) of the Income-tax Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2026.

entries.title: TDS on transfer of immovable property
entries.body: Any person (transferee) buying immovable property (other than agricultural land) from a resident must deduct TDS at the time of credit or payment. Reported via Form 26QB.
entries.threshold: Consideration OR stamp-duty value of Rs 50,00,000 or more (whichever is higher). If either value is Rs 50 lakh or more, TDS applies on the higher of the two; no TDS only if BOTH are below Rs 50 lakh.
entries.payer: Transferee / buyer (any person, including individuals — no tax-audit precondition)

entries.caveats: Finance/No.2 Act 2024 (w.e.f. 01-10-2024) clarified that the 1% applies on the HIGHER of consideration or stamp-duty value, and that where there are multiple transferors/transferees the Rs 50 lakh test uses aggregate consideration. Excludes agricultural land. Buyer needs no TAN (uses Form 26QB). entries.title: TDS on professional or technical services
entries.body: Any person (other than individual/HUF not under tax audit) paying a resident fees for professional services, fees for technical services, royalty, or non-compete sums must deduct TDS at credit or payment, whichever is earlier.
entries.rate: 10% in general (professional fees, royalty, non-compete). 2% for fees for technical services (FTS), royalty for sale/distribution/exhibition of cinematographic films, and payees engaged solely in the business of operating a call centre.
entries.threshold: Rs 50,000 per financial year per category (raised from Rs 30,000 by the Finance Act 2025 w.e.f. 01-04-2025). The Rs 50,000 limit applies separately to each item (professional fees, FTS, royalty, sec 28(va) sums).
entries.payer: Person paying professional/technical fees (companies, firms, individuals/HUF under tax audit)
entries.caveats: Threshold raised from Rs 30,000 to Rs 50,000 (per category) w.e.f. 01-04-2025 (Finance Act 2025) — many charts still show Rs 30,000 (stale). entries.title: TDS on benefits or perquisites
entries.body: Any person providing a resident a benefit or perquisite (whether convertible into money or not) arising from that person's business or profession must deduct TDS on the value of the benefit. Covers free samples, sponsored trips, incentives in kind, etc.

entries.title: TDS on payments to non-residents
entries.body: Any person paying a non-resident (or foreign company) any sum chargeable to tax in India (other than salary) must deduct TDS at the rates in force. A catch-all section for cross-border payments; rate depends on the nature of income and any applicable tax treaty.
entries.rate: Varies by nature of income — there is no single rate. Common 'rates in force' include 20% (royalty/FTS to non-corporate non-residents, subject to change), 10% (interest on certain foreign-currency borrowings), 12.5% (long-term capital gains, post-Budget-2024 regime), and 30%/40% on other income depending on payee — OR the beneficial DTAA rate.
entries.rate_no_pan: Sec 206AA: higher of 'rate in force' or 20%. Relief: under Rule 37BC, no-PAN 20% may not apply to certain payments (interest, royalty, FTS, capital gains, dividend) if the non-resident furnishes prescribed details (TRC, address, etc.).
entries.threshold: No monetary threshold — TDS applies on the whole sum chargeable to tax, however small.
entries.payer: Any person (resident or non-resident) making the payment

entries.body: GSTR-1 reports outward supplies (sales). Taxpayers with aggregate annual turnover above Rs 5 crore, and those not opting for QRMP, must file it monthly.

entries.body: GSTR-9 is the GST annual return consolidating the year's outward/inward supplies, tax paid and ITC. It is filed once per financial year.
entries.rate: Due 31 December following the end of the financial year (e.g. FY 2025-26 -> 31 December 2026).

entries.caveats: The Rs 2 crore exemption is renewed by CBIC notification year-on-year (e.g. Notn 15/2025-CT for FY 2024-25); CA should confirm a corresponding exemption notification has been issued for FY 2025-26 before treating sub-Rs-2cr filing as optional. entries.title: Advance tax - 1st instalment (15%)
entries.body: Advance tax is paid in four instalments during the financial year by taxpayers whose net tax liability is Rs 10,000 or more.

entries.threshold: Net tax payable (after TDS/TCS) of Rs 10,000 or more in the year. Resident senior citizens (60+) with no business/professional income are exempt from advance tax.
entries.caveats: Standard cyclical date. Presumptive-income taxpayers (Sec 58, ex-44AD/44ADA) pay 100% in a single instalment by 15 March instead.

entries.title: GST registration threshold — goods (normal states)
entries.body: A supplier exclusively of goods must obtain GST registration once aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds the threshold. This Rs 40 lakh limit applies in 'normal' (non-special-category) states/UTs and was NOT changed by the GST 2.0 reforms of Sept 2025.
entries.rate: Registration mandatory above the threshold (Section 22, CGST Act).
entries.threshold: Rs 40,00,000 aggregate turnover (exclusive supply of goods, normal-category states)

entries.caveats: The Rs 40L goods limit is NOT automatic for all states — it applies only where the state adopted it (most normal states did via Notif 10/2019-CT). It is unavailable to: persons making inter-state supplies, those required to register compulsorily under Sec 24, ice-cream/pan-masala/tobacco suppliers, and anyone also supplying services beyond the de-minimis. GST 2.0 (56th Council, eff 22-09-2025) did NOT change registration thresholds — confirm the supplier deals ONLY in goods, else the Rs 20L services limit governs.
reviewFlags: Confirm the supplier deals EXCLUSIVELY in goods (any service supply beyond the de-minimis pushes the whole turnover to the Rs 20L services threshold).

Confirm none of the Sec 24 compulsory-registration triggers apply (they override the threshold entirely).

Threshold: Rs 20,00,000 aggregate turnover (services, or mixed goods+services, normal-category states) registration threshold services section-22

entries.title: GST registration threshold — special-category states
entries.body: Specified hilly/north-eastern states have lower registration thresholds: Rs 20 lakh for goods and Rs 10 lakh for services. The states at the lowest Rs 10L services tier include Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura.
entries.rate: Registration mandatory above the (lower) threshold (Section 22, CGST Act).
entries.threshold: Rs 20,00,000 for goods; Rs 10,00,000 for services (special-category states)

sources.name: ClearTax — GST registration threshold limits (special-category list)

entries.caveats: State-by-state mapping is the trap. The Rs 10L (services) / Rs 20L (goods) tier applies to Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura. Several states classified 'special category' under Art 279A actually OPTED for the Rs 40L goods limit (e.g. Jammu & Kashmir, Assam, Ladakh) or sit at Rs 20L for goods (Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Puducherry, Uttarakhand). A CA must confirm the specific state's adopted threshold from the relevant state notification before advising — the Art 279A list and the GST-threshold list are NOT identical.
reviewFlags: Confirm the SPECIFIC state's adopted threshold from that state's own notification — the Art 279A special-category list and the GST-threshold list are NOT identical, and several special-category states opted up to Rs 20L or Rs 40L for goods.

entries.title: Aggregate turnover — basis for thresholds
entries.body: All GST registration and composition thresholds are tested against 'aggregate turnover', which is computed PAN-India (all GSTINs of the same PAN combined), not per-state. It includes taxable, exempt, export and inter-state supplies, but excludes GST itself and inward RCM supplies.
entries.rate: Definitional — Section 2(6), CGST Act.
entries.threshold: None (defines how thresholds are measured)

sources.name: ClearTax — GST registration limits (aggregate turnover basis)

entries.caveats: A common error is measuring turnover per-state — it is PAN-level. Exempt supplies COUNT toward the registration threshold but interest/discount on deposits/loans is excluded from aggregate turnover for the composition-eligibility test (Sec 10 proviso). Confirm whether the client has multiple GSTINs under one PAN before concluding they are below a threshold.

entries.title: Simplified GST registration for small/low-risk taxpayers (Rule 14A)
entries.body: A GST 2.0 trade-facilitation measure: a voluntary fast-track registration granting automated approval within 3 working days for applicants whose monthly output tax liability (CGST+SGST/UTGST+IGST+cess) does not exceed Rs 2.5 lakh. Introduced by Notif 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31-10-2025 (new Rule 14A, with the Rule 9A procedure, in the CGST Rules).
entries.rate: Auto-approval within 3 working days, subject to Aadhaar authentication and risk analytics.
entries.threshold: Monthly output tax liability up to Rs 2,50,000 (self-assessed)

entries.title: Composition scheme eligibility — traders / manufacturers
entries.body: The composition scheme (Section 10, CGST Act) lets small suppliers of goods (and restaurants) pay tax at a flat rate on turnover with simplified quarterly payment (CMP-08) and annual return (GSTR-4), but they cannot collect GST or claim input tax credit. The turnover limit is Rs 1.5 crore (Rs 75 lakh in specified special-category states).
entries.rate: Eligibility provision; flat rates apply (see separate rate entries).
entries.threshold: Aggregate turnover up to Rs 1,50,00,000 (Rs 75,00,000 in specified special-category states) in the preceding FY

sources.name: Indian Tax Update — Section 10 composition levy (2025 updates)

entries.caveats: Limit and rates were NOT changed by GST 2.0. Ineligible: inter-state outward suppliers, e-commerce suppliers (those required to collect TCS), manufacturers of ice-cream, pan-masala, tobacco, aerated water and (per later notifications) certain other goods, and casual/non-resident taxable persons. A composition trader/manufacturer may supply services only up to 10% of turnover or Rs 5 lakh, whichever is higher. The Rs 75L special-category sub-limit applies to a specific subset of states — confirm the state.
reviewFlags: Confirm the client falls in none of the ineligibility buckets (inter-state outward supply, supply via TCS-collecting e-commerce operator, notified excluded manufacture, casual/non-resident taxable person).
Confirm whether the Rs 1.5cr or the Rs 75L sub-limit applies for the client's specific state — the Rs 75L tier covers only a subset of special-category states.

entries.title: Composition rate — traders (goods dealers)
entries.body: A composition dealer trading in goods pays 1% of taxable turnover within the state (0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST). Tax is on taxable turnover of goods, not exempt turnover.
entries.rate: 1% of taxable turnover (0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST)
entries.threshold: Eligible up to Rs 1.5 crore aggregate turnover (see eligibility entry)

sources.name: Indian Tax Update — Section 10 composition rates

entries.caveats: For a TRADER the 1% is on turnover of TAXABLE goods only (exempt turnover excluded); for a MANUFACTURER the 1% is on total turnover. GST 2.0 rate rationalisation (new 5%/18%/40% slabs) did NOT touch composition rates — those flow from Section 10 read with Notif 8/2017-CT, unaffected by the rate-slab changes.
reviewFlags: Confirm the base for the 1%: TAXABLE turnover for a trader vs TOTAL turnover for a manufacturer — applying the wrong base mis-states the liability.

entries.title: Composition rate — restaurants (non-alcohol)
entries.body: Restaurants and other suppliers of food/drink for human consumption (not serving alcoholic liquor) opting for composition pay 5% of turnover (2.5% CGST + 2.5% SGST).
entries.rate: 5% of turnover (2.5% CGST + 2.5% SGST)

sources.name: ClearTax — impact of GST on restaurant / food services ('specified premises')

entries.caveats: Only restaurants NOT serving alcoholic liquor for human consumption qualify. This is distinct from regular (non-composition) restaurant supply: a standalone restaurant is generally 5% without ITC, while restaurant service in 'specified premises' (a hotel with room tariff above Rs 7,500/day) is 18% with ITC. Note the 55th GST Council replaced the old 'declared tariff' concept with the actual-tariff 'specified premises' test effective 01-04-2025 — do NOT use the stale 'declared/specified-tariff hotel' phrasing. The 5% composition restaurant rate itself was unchanged by GST 2.0.
reviewFlags: Confirm the client serves NO alcoholic liquor for human consumption (alcohol service disqualifies the composition restaurant rate).

entries.title: Composition scheme for service providers (Section 10(2A))
entries.body: A separate composition-type scheme lets small service providers (and mixed suppliers) not eligible for the goods scheme pay 6% (3% CGST + 3% SGST) on first supplies, if aggregate turnover in the preceding FY was up to Rs 50 lakh. Introduced by Notif 2/2019-CT(R) and given statutory force as Section 10(2A).
entries.rate: 6% of turnover (3% CGST + 3% SGST)
entries.threshold: Aggregate turnover up to Rs 50,00,000 in the preceding financial year

entries.title: Special composition scheme — bricks
entries.body: Brick manufacturers/traders (building bricks, fly-ash bricks/blocks, roofing tiles, earthen/roofing tiles) operate under a special scheme: either 6% GST without ITC, or 12% GST with ITC. The registration threshold is a reduced Rs 20 lakh (not Rs 40 lakh). This scheme continues under GST 2.0.

entries.threshold: Registration mandatory above Rs 20,00,000 turnover (reduced threshold for this sector)

entries.title: GST 2.0 rate slabs (effective 22 Sept 2025)
entries.body: The 56th GST Council (3 Sept 2025) rationalised the rate structure into two principal slabs of 5% and 18%, with a 40% de-merit rate for luxury/sin goods, plus the existing nil (0%) category and special rates (e.g. 3% on gold/silver, 0.25% on rough diamonds). The 12% and 28% slabs were abolished; compensation cess on most goods was discontinued from 22 Sept 2025.
entries.rate: 0% (nil), 5%, 18%, 40% (de-merit); special rates 3% / 0.25% retained
entries.threshold: None (general rate structure)
entries.caveats: Do NOT quote pre-2025 12%/28% slabs — they no longer exist. Item-wise reclassification is large (most 12% goods to 5%, most 28% goods to 18%, ~10% of 28% goods to 40%); always verify the specific HSN against Notif 9/2025-CT(R). Compensation cess was discontinued for most goods from 22-09-2025 but continues on certain tobacco/pan-masala pending loan-repayment cessation — check current cess notifications for those items.
reviewFlags: For any specific item, verify the exact HSN-wise rate against Notif 9/2025-CT(R) — the 12%→5% / 28%→18% / 28%→40% reclassification is item-specific.
For tobacco/pan-masala, confirm whether compensation cess still applies (it continues on certain such items pending loan-repayment cessation, unlike most goods where cess ended 22-09-2025).

entries.body: Staple foods such as cereals, pulses, wheat/rice flour (atta/maida), when supplied loose / unbranded / not pre-packaged-and-labelled, are nil-rated. The same items become taxable (typically 5%) when supplied 'pre-packaged and labelled' within the meaning of the Legal Metrology Act (broadly, packs up to 25 kg / 25 litres).

entries.title: Exempt — individual life & health insurance (GST 2.0)
entries.body: A flagship GST 2.0 change: all INDIVIDUAL life insurance and INDIVIDUAL health insurance policies (including family-floater plans and reinsurance thereof) are exempt from GST, reduced from 18% to nil. entries.title: Nil-rated vs exempt vs non-taxable vs zero-rated
entries.body: 'Exempt supply' (Sec 2(47)) is an umbrella covering nil-rated, wholly-exempt and non-taxable supplies — none of which carry GST and none allow ITC on related inputs. This is distinct from 'zero-rated' supply (exports / SEZ supplies under Sec 16 IGST Act), which carries a 0% effective rate BUT preserves ITC / refund.
entries.rate: Exempt/nil = 0% with NO ITC; zero-rated = 0% WITH ITC/refund
entries.threshold: None (definitional)

sources.name: ClearTax — exemptions under GST (nil vs exempt)

entries.caveats: The practical trap is ITC: a supplier of exempt/nil goods must REVERSE/restrict ITC under Sec 17(2) and Rule 42/43, whereas a zero-rated (export) supplier keeps full ITC and can claim refund. entries.title: E-way bill threshold — Rs 50,000
entries.body: An e-way bill (EWB-01) is required for movement of goods where the consignment value exceeds Rs 50,000, under Section 68 read with Rule 138 of the CGST Rules. It is mandatory for inter-state movement above this value; for intra-state movement the threshold is the same Rs 50,000 in most states, though some states use a higher intra-state limit.

entries.title: E-way bill validity period
entries.body: E-way bill validity runs from the time Part-B (vehicle details) is first entered: one day for every 200 km (or part thereof) for regular cargo, and one day for every 20 km (or part thereof) for Over-Dimensional Cargo (ODC). A 'day' ends at midnight of the following day from generation time.

entries.caveats: The 200 km/day figure has applied since 01-01-2021 (earlier it was 100 km/day) — stale references quoting 100 km/day are wrong. Two 2025 controls also apply: an EWB can be generated only for documents dated within 180 days of generation (from 01-01-2025), and validity extension is capped at 360 days from original generation (from 01-01-2025). Validity can be extended only within the window (8 hrs before to 8 hrs after expiry).

entries.title: GST rate slabs after GST 2.0 (Sept 2025)
entries.body: From 22 Sep 2025 the GST Council rationalised slabs into a simplified structure: a 5% 'merit' rate and an 18% 'standard' rate for the bulk of goods, plus Nil (exempt) for essentials and a 40% 'demerit/sin' rate for luxury and sin goods. The earlier 12% and 28% slabs were abolished.

Always classify by HSN against Notification 09/2025-CT(Rate), which supersedes 01/2017-CT(Rate).

entries.title: What reverse charge (RCM) is, and the two legal hooks
entries.body: Under reverse charge the recipient of the supply, not the supplier, pays GST directly to the government and self-invoices. Two enabling provisions exist: Sec 9(3) CGST / Sec 5(3) IGST (notified categories of goods and services) and Sec 9(4) CGST / Sec 5(4) IGST (notified supplies received by a registered person from an unregistered supplier).
entries.rate: No single rate. RCM applies the same GST rate that the underlying goods/service would bear; the recipient pays it in cash (RCM liability cannot be set off against ITC) and may then claim ITC if otherwise eligible.
entries.threshold: None for Sec 9(3) notified supplies (applies from rupee one once the recipient is covered). Sec 9(4) applies only to specifically notified classes (e.g. promoter shortfall purchases, metal scrap from unregistered persons).

sources.name: ClearTax — Sec 16(4) of CGST Act / RCM ITC timing
sources.ref: CBIC Circular 211/5/2024-GST — Sec 16(4) relevant FY for RCM self-invoices

entries.caveats: RCM tax must be paid in cash, not by utilising ITC; ITC of the RCM tax is then available to the recipient subject to the usual conditions and the time limit in Sec 16(4). For RCM on supplies from unregistered persons, the Sec 16(4) 'relevant FY' for the ITC time limit is the FY in which the recipient issues the self-invoice (CBIC Circular 211/5/2024-GST). The 56th Council 'GST 2.0' rate rationalisation (w.e.f. 22-09-2025) reshaped the rate slabs but did NOT alter the RCM mechanism or the lists in Notif 13/2017 and 4/2017. CA must confirm self-invoicing (Sec 31(3)(f)) and payment-voucher compliance for each RCM inward supply.

entries.title: Goods Transport Agency (GTA) road transport
entries.body: Where a GTA transports goods by road and has NOT opted to pay under forward charge, the specified recipient pays GST under RCM. entries.rate: 18% under RCM for most such services (rate follows the specific service).

entries.title: GTA under RCM - 5% (recipient pays)
entries.body: Goods Transport Agency (GTA) road-freight service to notified recipients (companies, registered persons, factories, body corporates, etc.) is taxed at 5% under reverse charge - the recipient pays the 5% and may claim ITC. The earlier 12%-with-ITC option was abolished under GST 2.0; the 5% concessional route continues. There is no longer any per-consignment value exemption: both the old Rs 1,500 (single-carriage) and Rs 750 (single-consignee) exemptions were WITHDRAWN with effect from 18 July 2022, so every GTA consignment is now taxable regardless of value (unless the goods themselves are in the exempt specified-goods list).

entries.title: Renting residential dwelling for residence - exempt (RCM if to registered person)
entries.body: Renting a residential dwelling for use as a residence is exempt when let to an unregistered person. entries.title: Income-tax Act 2025 governs FY 2026-27
entries.body: FY 2026-27 (AY 2027-28 / Tax Year 2026-27) is assessed under the Income-tax Act 2025, which came into force on 01-04-2026 and replaced the Income-tax Act 1961. entries.title: s.87A rebate (new regime) - income up to Rs 12 lakh tax-free
entries.body: Under the new regime, a resident individual whose total income does not exceed Rs 12,00,000 gets a rebate equal to the tax payable, capped at Rs 60,000 - making such income effectively tax-free. entries.title: 80D - health insurance premium (old regime only)
entries.body: Section 80D (s.126 under the Income-tax Act 2025) allows a deduction for health-insurance premiums and preventive health check-ups. Limits depend on age. Available ONLY in the old regime.
entries.rate: Self/spouse/dependent children: up to Rs 25,000 (Rs 50,000 if the eldest insured is a senior citizen). Parents: additional Rs 25,000 (Rs 50,000 if senior). Preventive check-up up to Rs 5,000 is within these caps. So max Rs 1,00,000 where both self and parents are seniors.
entries.threshold: Rs 25,000 / Rs 50,000 per group as above

entries.title: 80CCD(1B) - extra Rs 50,000 NPS (old regime only)
entries.body: Section 80CCD(1B) (s.124 under the Income-tax Act 2025) gives an ADDITIONAL deduction of up to Rs 50,000 for the individual's own NPS contribution, over and above the Rs 1.5 lakh 80C ceiling. Available ONLY in the old regime.

entries.title: 80CCD(2) - employer NPS contribution (both regimes)
entries.body: Section 80CCD(2) allows a deduction for the EMPLOYER's contribution to the employee's NPS account. Unlike most Chapter VI-A deductions, this one IS available under the new regime, and at a higher 14% limit.
entries.rate: Up to 14% of salary (Basic + DA) in the new regime for all employees; 10% of salary under the old regime (14% for central/state government employees). Outside the Rs 1.5L cap.
entries.threshold: 14% (new regime) / 10% (old regime, non-govt) of Basic + DA
entries.caveats: One of the very few deductions surviving in the new regime. From FY 2025-26 the 14% limit was extended to all (not just govt) employees under the new regime; old regime stays at 10% for non-govt. 'Salary' = Basic + DA (forming part of retirement benefits).

entries.title: 24(b) - home-loan interest, Rs 2 lakh (self-occupied, old regime)
entries.body: Section 24(b) (s.72 under the Income-tax Act 2025) allows a deduction for interest on a housing loan. For a self-occupied property the cap is Rs 2,00,000 a year and is available ONLY in the old regime. For a let-out property the full interest is deductible (subject to the house-property loss set-off cap).
entries.rate: Self-occupied: up to Rs 2,00,000 (old regime only; NOT allowed in new regime). Let-out: full interest deductible (set-off of house-property loss against other heads capped at Rs 2,00,000/year).
entries.threshold: Rs 2,00,000 (self-occupied)

entries.caveats: Self-occupied interest is barred in the new regime; let-out-property interest is deductible in the new regime too, but the resulting house-property LOSS generally cannot be set off against other heads in the new regime (set-off against other heads is capped at Rs 2,00,000/yr, excess carried forward 8 years). entries.title: Advance-tax instalment due dates FY 2026-27
entries.body: Any taxpayer whose estimated tax liability for the year is Rs 10,000 or more must pay advance tax in four instalments (s.408 of the Income-tax Act 2025, old s.211). Cumulative percentages apply.
entries.rate: 15 Jun 2026: 15% cumulative | 15 Sep 2026: 45% cumulative | 15 Dec 2026: 75% cumulative | 15 Mar 2027: 100%. Shortfall/deferment attracts interest at 1% per month (deferment interest = s.425, old s.234C; default interest = old s.234B, in the same advance-tax cluster of the 2025 Act).
entries.threshold: Estimated annual tax liability >= Rs 10,000
entries.caveats: Resident senior citizens (60+) with NO business/professional income are exempt from advance tax. Presumptive taxpayers (old 44AD/44ADA, now s.58) pay 100% in a single instalment by 15 Mar 2027. Interest: the 1%/month deferment interest is s.425 (old s.234C) under the 2025 Act; the default-interest section (old s.234B) sits in the same cluster (~s.424) but its exact number is not yet pinned - CA to confirm against the bare 2025-Act.
reviewFlags: Confirm the exact 2025-Act section number for default interest (old s.234B). Verifier pinned deferment interest (old s.234C) to s.425 but could only place s.234B approximately at ~s.424.

entries.title: New regime is default; opting for old regime
entries.body: From AY 2024-25 onwards the new regime is the DEFAULT. To use the old regime a taxpayer must affirmatively opt out. Salaried taxpayers (no business income) can choose every year via the ITR. Those with business/professional income must file Form 10-IEA (or its 2025-Act successor) to opt out and can switch back only once.
entries.rate: Default = new regime. Old regime = opt-in (annual for non-business; restricted switching for business income via the prescribed form).
